title: The Books Your CEO Has Already Read
author: Is It Working?
summary: Senior leaders across functions share a common management canon—Porter, Collins, Kaplan, Lencioni, Kotter, Drucker—but HR and communications professionals often haven't read it, creating a vocabulary gap that limits their influence in strategic conversations. When a CEO talks about competitive advantage, they're drawing on Porter. When they discuss team dysfunction, they mean Lencioni. Not knowing these texts means you can do your job but won't always follow or lead the conversation. The article profiles five modern classics plus one underread classic (Drucker's The Effective Executive) as the essential shared library that closes the gap between functional expertise and strategic credibility.
points: Many HR and communications professionals lack the management canon their CEOs operate from—Porter on strategy, Kaplan on measurement, Lencioni on team dysfunction, Kotter on change—creating a vocabulary gap that limits their strategic influence.
Collins's Good to Great showed that great company performance came from disciplined people, disciplined thought, and disciplined action—not dramatic leadership or technology.
Porter's competitive advantage framework holds that sustainable advantage requires genuine choice: you cannot be all things, and neither can your organization.

Lencioni's five team dysfunctions (absence of trust, fear of conflict, lack of commitment, avoidance of accountability, inattention to results) remain the standard boardroom language for team failure.
Drucker's Effective Executive argues that effectiveness is a discipline, not a talent—and can be learned; most executives, he showed, are wrong about where their time actually goes.
quotes: Senior leaders share a common library. However, many HR and communications professionals haven’t read it.
If you haven’t read those books, you’re working with a vocabulary you only half understand. You can still do your job, but you won’t always follow the conversation. And you’ll rarely lead it.
His core point is simple: sustainable advantage requires choice. You cannot be all things and neither can your organisation.
The argument is that most teams fail for predictable reasons: absence of trust, fear of conflict, lack of commitment, avoidance of accountability, inattention to results.

His eight-step model (build urgency, form a coalition, create a vision, communicate it, remove obstacles, secure early wins, sustain momentum, make it stick) became the standard reference for every major transformation.
His argument is superbly precise: effectiveness is a discipline, not a talent and it can be learned.
